newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FEATURE - African nightclubs booming in Lisbon.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - African nightclubs booming in Lisbon.

text.p: Everyone is welcome at the African nightclubs of Lisbon where blacks and whites listen to the beat from Angola, Mozambique and Cape Verde, and dance the night away.
This is not Harlem or Brixton. No racial tensions here. People just want to feel the music.
The heyday of the African nightclub in Lisbon has arrived. Immigrants dress up in berets, shiny suits and bright shirts and parade the dance floor in tropical style.
Two dozen African nightclubs are scattered across the city, smoky places with potted palms where immigrants remember home and the Portuguese get nostalgic about colonial times.
"The Portuguese still feel strong ties to Africa because of their colonial past," said Vitor Trindade, owner of two African nightclubs in Lisbon.
"The African clubs reflect the Portuguese people's love of Africa and the Africans' pride in their culture and memories of their homeland."
He said the boom in African nightclubs began about three years ago as the Portuguese economy picked up.
Jose Eduardo Agualusa, an Angolan writer who has written a book about the lives of Africans in Lisbon, said: "The clubs are places for Africans to meet in a relaxed atmosphere."

At the "Ritz Club" in the red light district of Lisbon, white Portuguese and Africans from the former colonies of Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau and Sao Tome and Principe join hands and dance before a live band.
A few American tourists who stumbled on the club found a table and some drinks, and joined the crowd on the oak dance floor in a fog of tobacco smoke.

"At one table you see a poor man, at another the 'jet set', and at another some intellectuals. You get everyone here. They all come for the beat," said nightclub minder and singer Andre Cabaco from Mozambique.

The "Ritz Club" in an old part of the capital where the laundry hangs out of the windows above the street is a respectable place, unlike the dozens of bars nearby where drug-addicted prostitutes ply their trade.
At "Mussulo", a discotheque with an Angolan flavour in the commercial district, there were few white faces among some 300 blacks but no one batted an eyelid.
RACIAL HARMONY REFLECTS COUNTRY AS A WHOLE
Trindade said the racial harmony among the customers of the African night clubs reflected Portuguese society as a whole.

The beating to death of a young black man from Cape Verde by skinheads in central Lisbon in June 1995 was an isolated incident, residents say. A group of skinheads is now on trial for the killing and the verdict is due in a few weeks.
The African nightclubs are drug-free, unlike other nightspots in Lisbon where the problem is rife, nightclub workers and residents say.
People frequent the clubs to enjoy the best of African music, like Angola's "Kizomba", Mozambique's "Marrabentas" and Cape Verde's "Funana".
"I just love the music here. It makes me think of where I'm from," said Mina Lima, a 20-year-old Cape Verdean student, as she twisted to the deafening rhythms at "Mussulo".
Clubs quickly go out of fashion as new ones spring up. The latest "in" spot is "Kamanga" downtown, according to devotees. Some clubs cater for older people and others for the young, smart set.
A different band plays every night at spots such as "Kussunguila" and "Beleza" from about one a.m. -- always late even in midweek -- until four a.m. when the clubs close.
Fridays and Saturdays are the busiest. The customers who keep the clubs ticking during the week are mainly students.

Bands with names like "Bonga" and "Kussonolola" are comprised of Angolans, Mozambicans, Cape Verdeans and Guineans, whose families probably settled in Lisbon after the colonial wars of the 1960s and 1970s ended with independence.
The bands often include Brazilian and other South American music in their repertoires.
Foreign tourists discovered the African nightclubs more by word of mouth than through write-ups in tour guides, Trindade said. "The Scandinavians especially love the beat," he added.

The entry charge to the clubs ranges between 1,500 and 3,000 escudos ($9-18) per person, which includes a couple of alcoholic drinks, a fraction of the price to get into a chic nightspot in New York or London.
